name: ispell
why: A decades-old spell checker with a deep lineage, though mostly plumbing now.

brief.what_it_is: International Ispell is an interactive, screen-oriented spell checker for Unix that supports many European languages. It reads a text file and shows each error in the context of the original file, then suggests corrections when it can work them out. It has an Emacs interface (ispell.el) as well as a standard command-line mode, and the Kspell graphical front end is mentioned on the page. The homepage does not say what the Homebrew package adds beyond the main program, but the executable list includes helper tools such as buildhash, findaffix, munchlist, and tryaffix that the page does not describe.
brief.why_it_exists: The page frames ispell as a faster and easier alternative to Unix spell that can handle languages other than English. It also notes that Aspell, by Kevin Atkinson, is better at suggesting corrections for badly misspelled words, while ispell's approximate matching is English-specific.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internals. It says the affix-file format is documented in the distribution's Unix man pages, so dictionaries are driven by affix files. Helper executables such as buildhash and munchlist appear to be part of building dictionaries, but the page does not confirm this.

commands_seen.context: Prints the full version string, 'International Ispell Version x.y.z', which the page asks people to cite in scholarly work.
Opens the Unix manual page for ispell, which the page says ships with the distribution and includes the affix-file format docs.

brief.install_notes: The page says Mac OS X works but you need the Xcode developer tools installed, and /usr/local/bin must be in your PATH after installing. English American and British dictionaries come with ispell. Other languages need separate dictionaries from a list the page links to, and the emacs ispell.el interface is usually bundled with Emacs. For Microsoft platforms the page says there are compile options in the pc/README file in the distribution.
brief.standout: The project has a long lineage: the page says the original was written in PDP-10 assembly in 1971, the C version came from MIT, and the current release is by Geoff Kuenning. The page also gives explicit citation guidance, noting that there is no published paper and asking users to cite the full version number.
brief.status: Maintained by the author as of the page, which lists version 3.4.06 as current and says the page is maintained by Geoff Kuenning. The page gives no release date and no commit history, so the exact recency is unknown. The page says 'After a long hiatus, Ispell 3.4 primarily offers bug fixes, increased portability, and improved English dictionaries.' The brew scout note calls it 'mostly plumbing now', but the page itself does not say that.
brief.caveats: The page says ispell is not officially supported on Microsoft platforms. Mac support requires the Xcode developer tools and a PATH change. The page gives no licence information. Its online resources section also points to a JavaScript-dependent web spell checker that is not part of ispell. Bug reports go to itcorp.com addresses, and the page asks that add-on packages be reported to their own developers.
quotes: Ispell is a fast screen-oriented spelling checker that shows you your errors in the context of the original file, and suggests possible corrections when it can figure them out.
Ispell is a very old program.
There is no published paper on ispell, so if you make use of ispell in a fashion that requires a reference
